To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the official Russian view of Belarusians was a complex mixture of the “we” and “they” attitudes.

the Belarusians and Russians were two distinct peoples, that they were not, however, so distinct as to preclude them from belonging to a common nation, and that, finally, the differences between the two groups were such as to make them distinct enough to justify the creation of a distinct administrative entity for Belarus within the Russian empire.
the Belarusian intelligentsia was not only the most important factor in the development of a Belarusian national consciousness, but also the only one capable of developing it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What were the official Russian attitudes toward Belarusians?
the question of the extent to which official Russia was willing to recognize the existence of the Belarusian nation.
the following questions: How did the Russian imperial bureaucracy understand the relationship between Belarusians and Russians, and how did they define the borders of “Russianness”?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Belarusian people were considered a part of the “Russian” nation, but that the Belarusian nation was not considered identical with the “Russian” one.
the Belarusians were not “us” but not “them,” either, but rather “almost us.”
the Russian Empire was an empire of the Russian nation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Belarusians were considered by official Russia to be a “Russian” nationality.
the Belarusian national identity in the late nineteenth century was not yet a self-conscious one.
in the period from 1863 to 1914, the Russian government was unable to formulate a consistent policy toward Belarusian national identity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Russian state did not have a consistent or unified policy toward its Belarusian population.
the “Russian nation,” as understood and defined by the Russian state, was a very large, and very flexible, category.
, in the period between the Polish insurrection of 1863 and the First World War, the Belarusian national identity was not a fixed and stable category.
